strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely topic: extending self-play reinforcement learning in LLMs to multi-agent, multi-turn settings spanning both competitive and cooperative environments.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive in scope, evaluating agents on in-distribution games, out-of-distribution games, and downstream multi-agent LLM systems (MAD and AutoGen) across several reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, AIME, GPQA).

The paper provides an interesting qualitative analysis of emergent chain-of-thought patterns (role awareness, intent recognition) when transitioning from games to collaborative/competitive multi-agent tasks.
weaknesses: Technical novelty of the algorithmic contributions is limited. The 'sum-then-normalize' estimator is standard Monte Carlo return estimation (or GAE with gamma=1, lambda=1 with a batch-mean baseline), and agent-specific normalization is a standard practice in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) with asymmetric roles/payoffs.

Major contradictory results in the ablation studies: in Table 9 (MAD framework), removing the core components of MARS yields substantially higher downstream reasoning scores than the full proposed models (e.g., MARS Tic-Tac-Toe without turn-level advantage estimation achieves 60.00% on AIME and 47.98% on GPQA, compared to 43.33% and 41.12% for the full MARS Tic-Tac-Toe model). The text completely overlooks this contradiction and only discusses game returns from Table 4.

Plausibility and variance of transfer claims: Training on extremely simple toy games (Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker) is claimed to boost advanced reasoning on AIME24 and GPQA. Given that AIME consists of only 30 questions (where a single question shift represents 3.33%), the lack of error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance tests leaves it unclear whether gains are due to genuine strategic reasoning transfer or variance/length/prompt adherence artifacts.

Noticeable writing issues and unfinished text: the abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('Our code and models are publicly available a'), the Reproducibility Statement is missing the repository URL ('available at The repository includes'), and several typos exist in Section 3.1 ('A naive , we can consider') and Table 5 ('Dual Clip Loss ture', 'Lambd').

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and ambitious question: whether self-play reinforcement learning on strategic games (both cooperative and competitive) can instill multi-agent interaction capabilities that transfer to downstream reasoning workflows.
The framework incorporates both cooperative (Mini Hanabi) and competitive (Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker) games, extending beyond prior work that focused purely on two-player zero-sum games.
The manuscript provides extensive prompt specifications and implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Major empirical contradiction in ablation results: In Table 9 (evaluation under the MAD framework), models trained without the proposed turn-level advantage estimator or without agent-specific advantage normalization significantly outperform the complete MARS model across multiple benchmarks (e.g., on AIME, MARS (Tic.) achieves 43.33%, whereas '+ w/o turn-level' reaches 60.00% and '+ w/o agent-specific' reaches 56.67%; on GPQA, ablations reach 47.98%–50.00% vs. 41.12% for MARS). This directly contradicts the core claim in Section 4.5 that both components are essential and superior for multi-agent reasoning.

Theoretical flaw in advantage baseline computation: In Section 3.2, the advantage is defined as $A_{k,t}^i = R_k^i - \text{mean}(\mathbf{R})$, where $\mathbf{R}$ aggregates cumulative returns across all turns. Because cumulative returns naturally decrease over time in positive-reward settings ($R_k = \sum_{k'=k}^K r_{k'}$), normalizing against a global mean pooled over all turns introduces a systematic positive bias for early turns and a negative bias for late turns, rather than centering returns relative to a turn-specific value baseline $\mathbb{E}[R_k]$.

Plausibility and causal mechanism of downstream transfer: The training games (Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker, Mini Hanabi) have minute state spaces and trivial action sets. The paper claims that playing these toy games provides dramatic downstream gains on graduate-level reasoning benchmarks (e.g., AIME and GPQA-Diamond) inside multi-agent frameworks, yet in the single-agent setting (Table 1 and Table 8), MARS models actually degrade GPQA performance (dropping from 39.39% to 33.84%–36.36%). The paper lacks rigorous controls (such as length control, role-prompting SFT baselines, or standard RL fine-tuning on dialogue) to rule out superficial formatting or verbosity shifts.

Insufficient baselines: The only post-training comparison provided is SPIRAL; standard multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms, PPO with a learned critic, and direct supervised fine-tuning on multi-agent game traces are not evaluated.

strengths: The paper tackles a compelling and timely research question: extending end-to-end reinforcement learning with self-play to both cooperative and competitive multi-turn, multi-agent game settings for LLMs.

Unlike prior work (such as SPIRAL) that concentrates exclusively on two-player zero-sum adversarial games, MARS incorporates cooperative games (Hanabi) to encourage social reasoning, theory of mind, and collaboration.

The evaluation covers a wide range of settings, including game playing on both seen and held-out games (Connect Four, Leduc Hold'em, Simple Hanabi) as well as downstream reasoning benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, AQUA, AIME, AMC, MMLU, GPQA) across different multi-agent architectures (MAD, AutoGen).
Detailed prompt templates and training hyperparameters are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: Conceptual and technical novelty of the advantage estimation is limited: The proposed 'sum-then-normalize' turn-level advantage estimator is essentially standard Monte Carlo return-to-go estimation with baseline subtraction. Furthermore, subtracting a single pooled scalar mean(R^p) across all turns in Eq. (3) is statistically problematic for multi-turn episodes with intermediate rewards, because earlier turns accumulate more rewards and will be systematically biased upward relative to later turns.

Severe contradictions in downstream benchmark ablations: In Table 9 (evaluation within the MAD framework), models with the key proposed components removed ('+ w/o turn-level advantage estimator' and '+ w/o agent-specific advantage normalization') substantially and consistently outperform the full MARS models across nearly all benchmarks (for instance, AIME jumps from 43.33% in MARS (Tic.) to 60.00% without turn-level estimation, and GPQA jumps from 41.12% to 47.98%). The paper neither reports nor addresses why ablating the proposed core contributions leads to dramatically higher downstream performance.

Discrepancies between claims and reported numbers: The abstract and introduction claim performance gains of '12.5% on GPQA-Diamond', but Table 1 reports gains of only +7.57% under MAD (37.88% to 45.45%) and +2.53% under AutoGen (47.47% to 50.00%), while in the single-agent setting the generalist model actually degrades from 39.39% to 34.85%.

Evaluation rigor and variance: Downstream benchmarks with small test sets (such as AIME with ~30 problems) exhibit large variance where a change of a few solved problems causes swings of 10%+. No error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-seed trials are provided to demonstrate statistical significance.

Incomplete text and drafting errors: Several sentences are truncated or contain noticeable typos (e.g., the abstract cuts off abruptly with 'Our code and models are publicly available a'; the reproducibility statement has an empty link 'publicly available at The repository'; Table 5 has 'Dual Clip Loss ture' and 'Lambd').

strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: Investigating whether self-play reinforcement learning across both cooperative and competitive strategic games can instill generalizable multi-agent interaction skills in LLMs is an important and interesting research question.

Well-designed algorithmic adaptations: The paper cleanly identifies key challenges in multi-turn multi-agent GRPO (non-zero mean advantage instability when summing normalized turn rewards, and role-specific payoff variance) and introduces sensible, grounded remedies ('sum-then-normalize' cumulative returns and agent-specific normalization).

Extensive empirical evaluation: The evaluation covers both in-distribution and out-of-distribution games (Connect Four, Leduc Hold'em, Simple Hanabi) as well as downstream transfer to multi-agent frameworks (MAD and AutoGen) across math and QA benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, AQUA, AIME, AMC, MMLU, GPQA).

Insightful qualitative and behavioral analysis: The examination of reasoning traces (<think> tags) and the taxonomy-based failure mode analysis on GPQA-Diamond convincingly illustrate the specific reduction in 'Inter-Agent Misalignment' (e.g., reduced task derailment and better attention to partner input).
Comprehensive appendix: Includes scaling experiments to 8B models, controlled decoupling experiments against SPIRAL, direct comparisons to MT-GRPO, and hyperparameter sensitivity studies.
weaknesses: Unexplained discrepancies in ablation results: In Appendix Table 17 (downstream results in the MAD framework), several ablated variants—such as 'w/ Fixed Opponent' and 'w/o Turn-Level Advantage Estimator'—achieve substantially higher scores on AIME (e.g., 60.00% vs. 43.33%) and GPQA than the full MARSHAL model. This contradicts the narrative that these components are consistently beneficial and requires clear explanation or resolution.

Modest algorithmic novelty: The proposed turn-level advantage estimation is fundamentally a standard Monte Carlo return advantage estimator (equivalent to GAE with gamma=1, lambda=1) grouped by player role. While effective, the algorithmic innovation over existing RL formulations like GRPO and SPIRAL is relatively incremental.

Very small training environments: The environments used for training are toy games with extremely small state/action spaces (Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker, Mini Hanabi with only 8 cards total). It remains uncertain how well this self-play framework scales to environments with complex strategic dynamics, large action spaces, or more than two agents.

Potential evaluation variance on small benchmark subsets: Benchmarks like AIME24 have very small sample sizes (30 problems), where a 10% gain represents solving merely 3 additional problems. Reporting confidence intervals or multiple evaluation seeds would strengthen the claims of downstream transfer.

strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: Extending RLVR/GRPO from static, single-agent reasoning to multi-turn, multi-agent self-play addresses a crucial gap in LLM post-training.

Holistic game formulation: Unlike prior self-play works (e.g., SPAG, SPIRAL) which focus exclusively on competitive zero-sum games, MARSHAL thoughtfully integrates both competitive games and cooperative imperfect-information games (Hanabi), cultivating diverse capabilities like Theory of Mind, intent inference, and role adherence.

Principled and practical algorithmic adaptations: The proposed 'sum-then-normalize' turn-level advantage estimation and agent/role-specific normalization effectively resolve credit assignment and variance issues across asymmetric player roles in multi-turn environments.

Convincing transfer evaluation: Demonstrates clear generalization not only to more complex held-out games (Connect Four, Leduc Hold'em, Simple Hanabi) but also to practical multi-agent frameworks (competitive MAD debate and cooperative AutoGen) across challenging downstream reasoning benchmarks (e.g., AIME, GPQA-Diamond).

Insightful qualitative and error analyses: The categorization of failure modes (specifically showing significant drops in inter-agent misalignment) and reasoning trace analysis provide concrete evidence of how the learned game-theoretic behaviors translate into collaborative/adversarial reasoning.

Thorough supplementary studies: The appendix provides valuable extensions, including model scaling to Qwen3-8B, direct algorithmic decoupling from SPIRAL (RAE), and head-to-head empirical comparisons with concurrent MT-GRPO.
weaknesses: Anomalies in ablation results on downstream benchmarks: In Table 17 (MAD framework evaluation), several ablated models (such as models trained without turn-level advantage estimation or with a fixed opponent) achieve higher scores on difficult benchmarks like AIME and GPQA than the full MARSHAL models, which contradicts the main paper's claim and lacks discussion.

Scope of training environments: The training set relies on relatively small toy environments (Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker, Mini Hanabi). While effective for proof-of-concept, evaluating how well the framework scales to richer language-native sandboxes (e.g., text-based negotiation or software engineering workflows) remains future work.

Lack of error bars/variance reporting: Multi-agent self-play and downstream LLM evaluations often exhibit non-trivial variance across seeds; reporting standard deviations or confidence intervals across independent runs would strengthen the statistical rigor.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and timely research direction: extending end-to-end self-play reinforcement learning to multi-turn, multi-agent LLM systems across both competitive and cooperative game environments.

The evaluation covers a wide range of settings, including game-specific performance, out-of-distribution games (Connect Four, Leduc Hold'em, Simple Hanabi), and downstream reasoning benchmarks (AIME, GPQA, MATH) integrated into established multi-agent frameworks (MAD, AutoGen).

The inclusion of qualitative trace analysis and quantitative failure mode analysis (categorizing errors via the taxonomy of Cemri et al.) provides insightful perspectives on agent behavior during multi-turn interactions.
The submission includes extensive appendix material, featuring an 8B model scale-up, comparison against MT-GRPO, and full unnormalized reward tables.
weaknesses: Glaring contradictions between main claims and ablation results: In the main text (Section 4.5, Table 4), the authors claim that both the turn-level advantage estimator and agent-specific normalization are critical. However, Table 17 in the Appendix shows that removing either component substantially improves performance on downstream MAD benchmarks (e.g., AIME increases from 43.33% to 60.00% without turn-level advantage estimation, and GPQA increases from 41.12% to 47.98%). This strongly contradicts the paper's core hypothesis that these algorithmic modifications are the drivers of downstream reasoning gains.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed turn-level advantage estimator calculates the empirical Monte Carlo return from step k onward and subtracts the batch mean. This is standard textbook RL (equivalent to GAE with gamma=1, lambda=1 and an empirical baseline). Similarly, grouping advantages by player role is standard in multi-agent RL and closely mirrors concurrent work (e.g., Role-Conditioned Advantage Estimation in SPIRAL).

Degradation and noise on downstream general reasoning: In the standard single-agent setting (Table 1 and Table 16), MARSHAL models frequently degrade performance compared to the Qwen3-4B base model (e.g., the Generalist drops from 39.39% to 34.85% on GPQA and from 36.70% to 33.30% on AIME). Furthermore, on benchmarks with small test sets like AIME24 (30 problems), differences of 3.3% or 6.6% correspond to only 1–2 questions, yet no error bars, standard deviations, or multi-seed runs are reported.

Questionable causal connection between toy games and reasoning benchmarks: The training games (Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker, Mini Hanabi) have very small state/action spaces. Attributing improvements in complex STEM domains (e.g., AIME, GPQA) to 'Theory of Mind' and 'strategic skills' acquired from these toy games is weakly supported, especially when downstream improvements in multi-agent frameworks may simply arise from changes in response verbosity or formatting compliance caused by auxiliary rewards.
